#1456. Man United are a rotten, shambolic mess. They lack intelligence, look uncoached and fumbling, failing Michael Carrick is not the man to arrest this trauma, writes IAN LADYMAN

Published: 14:32 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 20:25 EST, 8 November 2026

Manchester United do not have a football team, more a collection of adrenaline junkies. Over time, it will not be enough.

So deficient are Michael Carrick's players that they surely can't keep their manager in a job for much longer. For the most part United are shambolic, a mess. At times they play football so devoid of intelligence and competence that it's almost impossible to fathom. They look uncoached.

Yet here they were for the second night running at Old Trafford, completing a lap of honour at full-time while their supporters sang the name of Carrick as he completed his own journey in front of the Stretford End towards the tunnel.

United – it's worth pointing out – are third bottom of the Premier League. They haven't won in the league since August and have conceded more goals across all competitions – 30 – than any team bar Crystal Palace in Europe's top divisions.

But at Old Trafford they will cling to anything to help them look in the mirror without laughing and currently the currency is comebacks. There was one against Roma in the Champions League last Tuesday and here – quite remarkably – there were two in one game.

None of it should really mean anything in the grand scheme. United are rotten, capable of playing effectively only when something gives them an energy spike with which to roll. It makes for quite hypnotic theatre but has inadequacy and desperation at its core.

Patrick Dorgu (centre) scored a late equaliser as troubled Man United drew 4-4 vs Aston Villa

Dorgu scored in the 96th-minute with this header but United sit 18th in the Premier League

Despite the draw, Michael Carrick's position as United head coach looks increasingly doubtful

It won't sustain them or indeed their fumbling, failing manager. But for the moment it's what they have and what they are.

MANCHESTER UNITED (4-2-3-1): Lammens 4; Mazraoui 4, Yoro 6, Maguire 5 (Heaven 46, 5), Dalot 3 (Dorgu 66, 8); Tielemans 6 (Mount 66, 5), Mainoo 6; Amad 5 (Lacey 66, 7), Fernandes 6, Cunha 7; Mbeumo 5 (Zirkzee 83, 7)

Goals: Fernandes (16 pen), Tielemans (44), Zirkzee (90+2), Dorgu (90+6)

ASTON VILLA (4-2-3-1): Suzuki 6; Harwood-Bellis 5, Lindelof 6, Torres 6, Maatsen 4; Goretzka 6 (Mbaye 78, 6), Kamara 4; Alysson 7 (Barkley 71, 6), McGinn 8 (Hemmings 71, 6), Manzambi 6; Jackson 6 (Madjo 86)

Goals: Alysson (1), Jackson (4), McGinn (48 pen), Goretzka (53)

Here, they twice trailed by two, at the start of both halves. They were 2-0 down after only four minutes and 4-2 behind after 53. Somehow they managed not to lose.

The two goals United scored in added time at the end of the game came from absolutely nowhere. On the touchline Carrick – free from total humiliation for the second time in six days – raised a single finger to the sky.

In the directors' box – where the TV companies seem to have a camera permanently trained these days – fist pumps were in evidence from those in United blazers.

This was another uncomfortable afternoon for Messrs Ratcliffe, Wilcox and Berrada. A collection of new banners in the crowd made feelings known.

For now, Carrick is being spared any of the blame. That is strange and wrong but tells us much about the confused nature of the modern United. If they blame one of their own then they really do have nowhere left to go in search of self-respect.

United's opening against Roma last week had been traumatic enough. This was even worse but the root of it was desperately familiar – incompetent football.

The hapless United full-back Diogo Dalot was to blame for the first goal as Villa's Brazilian Alysson blasted his shot through the Portuguese's limp challenge. Later – after conceding a second half penalty – Dalot was booed off by his own fans.

That was painful and unedifying but completely understandable. Dalot has played more than 250 games for United yet has never even been good enough.

Aston Villa took the lead after just 59 seconds when Alysson (centre) scored at Old Trafford

Nicolas Jackson (centre) doubled the visitors' lead on four minutes as they made a dream start

Bruno Fernandes pulled one back for the hosts with a penalty on 16 minutes in a crazy start

For goal two, goalkeeper Senne Lammens was culpable as he pushed Alysson's shot into the path of Nicolas Jackson.

Once again United were in sink or swim territory. Once again, amazingly, they kept their heads above water – at least for a while.

Boubacar Kamara's 13th minute challenge on Matheus Cunha was stupid as the Brazilian was heading away from goal. But the Bruno Fernandes penalty that followed was calm and precise and the shot of belief United needed was theirs.

For the next 20 minutes or so, Carrick's team played well off the back of it. It was the only part of their game that will look good on the highlights. The United front four pressed and harried the Villa defence to the extent that Unai Emery's team couldn't get up the field.

Villa keeper Zion Suzuki saved well from a Cunha curler while subsequent shots from Fernandes, Kobbie Mainoo and Amad Diallo took deflections and narrowly missed the target.

At some stage it felt as though United's energy must drop. Over time it did. But then they equalised.

Moments after seeing Suzuki save one of his own efforts, Amad found space to pull the ball back for Youri Tielemans who placed his first United goal in from 18 yards against his old club. Carrick's team deserved to be level at that stage and had played some enterprising football to get there. But their self-harm gene surfaced again before long.

Youri Tielemans (right) brought United level before half-time with this strike vs his old club

John McGinn put Villa ahead again just minutes after half-time from the penalty spot

Leon Goretkza (left) made it 4-2 to Villa with this close-range strike as they looked set to win

Joshua Zirkzee (left) pulled one back in second-half stoppage-time with this finish for United

Alysson had almost scored with the last big moment of the first half and in the 47th minute he drew an utterly dumb foul from Dalot and John McGinn scored the penalty firmly.

United are beyond compare in the Premier League when it comes to this kind of thing. Who else in the top flight concedes the kind of goals they do? A case in point came in the 53rd minute.

McGinn's free-kick was heading across goal and away when United defender Leny Yoro inexplicably headed it towards his own goal. Lammens somehow touched the ball on to the bar but when it dropped Leon Goretzka poked it in.

That was the 16th goal United had conceded in the last five games and this time the attempt at a fightback was more muted.

There were some half chances – shots from Cunha and Fernandes – and some territory in which to play.

But this was a game Villa were now able to control rather better and they looked set to ease home until Patrick Dorgu crossed for Joshua Zirkzee to ease a goal in from out of nothing in the 2nd minute of added time.

Old Trafford was emptying fast by the time Dorgu headed in a 96th equaliser from a corner. But by then the collective blood was up once more and it was enough.

Villa appealed for a foul on goalkeeper Suzuki and it's true Lammens had gone looking for him. Was the contact between the two 'keepers significant enough to warrant VAR intervention? Probably not. United had their draw and they had a point.

If the season ended today, they would be down. Yet they were cheered off. Some things you just can't make up.

#1455. Lethal Trent Alexander-Arnold sends Tuchel a statement in England victory

Thomas Tuchel has never been inclined to place much faith in the most famous right-back at his disposal, Trent Alexander-Arnold, once of Liverpool, now of Real Madrid, and – back in an England shirt – still capable of changing games in the blink of an eye.

England always looked likely to defeat a beleaguered Czech Republic team down to 10 men with just 25 minutes played, but it still required one man to conjure the moment of inspiration in this Nations League tie. This was the first cap in 15 months for the right-back now known simply as “Trent” in an England shirt – as well as his Real Madrid jersey – rather than the six syllables of his surname. With the game level at half-time, two minutes into the new half, he twice won the ball before landing a cross on the head of Anthony Gordon for the first goal.

TRENT ➡️ GORDON ⚽️🔥Anthony Gordon can't stop scoring for England, 3 goals in his last 3 games for England 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/xmqPIULJ24

Will the Alexander-Arnold with England experiment survive? One feels that Tuchel will need a little more to convince him to abandon whatever reservations he has about the Liverpudlian. A week short of his 28th birthday, Alexander-Arnold was winning just his 35th cap. His Real Madrid team-mate Jude Bellingham, a second-half substitute, was earning his 58th cap less than two months after his 23rd birthday. Bellingham was on as captain in place of the man he replaced, Harry Kane, scorer of England’s second. Bellingham’s international career has taken a much less rocky path than that of his Real team-mate.

Having missed the World Cup finals this summer, and had little good fortune around previous tournaments, one wonders if Euro 2028 might be the watershed moment for Alexander-Arnold. Either way, against opponents who sit back, he is lethal when it is time for the big delivery. Alexander-Arnold may not have the breadth of England experience that some of his peers have accumulated, but he does have plenty of experience of big games.

“I make that run time and time again,” Gordon said of his anticipation of the Alexander-Arnold cross, “but only a set number of players have that ability, that technique and the bravery to risk a mistake to play that pass. And that’s why I have been dying to play with him [Alexander-Arnold]. He’s been on his own journey but has trained really well this week. He should have played more. Sorry – he would have loved to have played more.”

A Freudian slip from the Barcelona winger, another Liverpudlian in Spain, who himself has barely put a foot wrong for England of late. He has three goals in three games for England, including the World Cup semi-final against Argentina. This was an England team that Tuchel fine-tuned, first to give a rest to Bellingham and in other quarters, too. Lewis Hall started at left-back. Trevoh Chalobah won his third England cap at centre-back. Alex Scott, of Bournemouth, was given his debut off the bench in the second half and Rio Ngumoha won the second cap of his England career, just one month after his 18th birthday.

As for Kane, his 87th goal for England now puts him within two goals of Robert Lewandowski, among four greats in the seven ahead of Kane on the all-time international goalscorers’ list. By the end of this international break the England captain should have equalled Peter Shilton’s record 125 caps. It has been an astonishing career even if it ends tomorrow. Following the missed penalty against Spain, Kane was again the man in the right place at the right time when Morgan Rogers’s shot was blocked in the second half.

“Strange to get an early red card,” Tuchel said. “Not the best for the team and spectators. It’s an awkward one, but we kept going, got a win and that’s what counts.” Not quite a vintage Czech Republic team, either, and when their best player of the opening stages, the attacking midfielder Pavel Sulc, of Lyon in Ligue 1, was dismissed after 25 minutes, it certainly did not become any easier for the home team. Sulc, the Czech player of the year in 2025, had mistimed a tackle on Elliot Anderson, which on a VAR review, the Turkish referee Umut Meler decided was worthy of an upgrade from yellow to red. It was high on the right calf of the England midfielder.

Czech Republic DOWN TO 10 MEN! 🟥Pavel Šulc sees red for a dangerous challenge on Elliot Anderson#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/B2YOLuS0vL

England had looked once more a little open to the counter-attack in the early stages, with Sulc one notable runner. This was not an opponent of the quality of Spain and Tuchel’s players were able to recover the situation. When they lose the ball in the opposition’s half, England tend to look vulnerable.

Even before the red card Rogers had hit a post. Myles Lewis-Skelly, playing in midfield, was booked for a foul on Lukas Serv and was pursued thereafter by the Czech players hoping to get an upgrade on the yellow card. He was substituted at half-time, with Eberechi Eze on in his place.

“I spoke to Ant [Gordon] at half-time,” Alexander-Arnold said later to ITV, “and I said if I’m getting in those spaces make sure you get to the back post. You don’t expect to get it that fast, but it did and it worked.”

Two minutes after the break, Alexander-Arnold suddenly burst into life. He won the ball back in his own area and then drove forward in search of the return. When that did not come, he raced back to win the ball again and unleashed one of those right-footed outswingers to the back post, where Gordon guided in the header. “Really proud to score that,” Gordon said, “because I can’t tell you the number of hours I’ve spent practising headers.”

Kane scored the second just a minute before he was replaced and Bellingham took the captain’s armband and the role as a No 9. One day someone will have to step into those goalscorer’s boots on a permanent basis and try to replace Kane – although it may be a while yet.

Thomas Tuchel has backed Jude Bellingham as a future England captain after giving him the armband in the victory over the Czech Republic.

In the absence of Declan Rice, who was vice-captain at the World Cup, Bellingham assumed the role when he came on for Harry Kane, who is now in his 10th season as England captain and also scored in the 2-0 win in Prague.

Tuchel, who needs to check on Bellingham ahead of Saturday’s game against Croatia after a “niggle,” has praised the midfielder’s attitude during the extended international break one year after he was back from an injury but left out of the squad.

“If you are the captain at the end of these matches, you can be the permanent captain,” Tuchel said when asked whether Bellingham could eventually lead the team. “He was the captain against New Zealand before the World Cup. It is always a reward and always an honour.

“I think he loves to be with us at the moment. That’s what I feel, and we had this small talk today about his role. We felt in our hearts or our stomachs to say ‘let’s go again, let’s start again’ and also our heads told us maybe 30 minutes is enough for this match because he hasn’t played in this quick turnaround through this season. He has done it before, but not in the season, so we didn’t want to be the first ones to try that.

“But even in this little encounter, you can see that he’s confident and happy to help from the bench. So it’s a reward. It’s good. He had a little niggle at the end of the match, so hopefully it’s nothing serious, and he’s available for Croatia.”

Nico O’Reilly is a doubt for the Croatia match in Rijeka and there are also concerns over Ezri Konsa, who was on the bench but not fit enough to play.

Trent Alexander-Arnold provided an assist for Anthony Gordon in the Real Madrid full-back’s first cap in 15 months. Gordon, meanwhile, has now scored in the first two Nations League games of the campaign and is staking his case to be an indispensable player for Tuchel.

“He’s getting there. He’s defending his shirt, he’s defending his position, an excellent performance again after his performance against Spain,” Tuchel said.

“He was very decisive today and had an excellent goal. It was very, very difficult, but the technique and finishing was excellent. He scored against Spain, so he has decisive actions and he’s defending his shirt and his position. He does it on the highest level and he’s a very important player.”

England returned to winning ways with a 2-0 win over Czech Republic in Prague.

Pavel Sulc’s first-half red card after a VAR review of his clumsy challenge on Elliot Anderson took the sting out of the initially lively hosts and Anthony Gordon gave Thomas Tuchel’s men a deserved lead early in the second half.

The forward headed home a fantastic cross by Trent Alexander-Arnold, who was making his first start under the German coach, before skipper Harry Kane scored to settle any nerves.

So who played well for England and who failed to impress? Rate each player with our voting tool, and have your say in the comments.

I thought we were very professional second half. We stepped up and needed to be more dynamic, bring more urgency into our play, which we did. We kept that intensity going and and the effort was till there. Deserved victory.

Strange to get an early red card. Not the best for the spectators, not the best for the team. It’s an awkward one. But we got the win.

To guide it into the goal, there was an awful lot [for Anthony Gordon] to do. Good pass, good goal. Both full-backs were good. The position in the second half suited Trent more than the position in the first half. Lewis was excellent on the other side.

We have used all the outfield players after two matches so credit to all of them. Now it’s important to relax and enjoy the evening, do a good recovery and prepare for Saturday.

I think it was good. They go down to 10 men and it should be easier for us to win the game, But in fact it makes it more difficult. They get very compact and defend with a lot of players around the box and it’s hard to break them down.

We got that [goal] at the start of the second half which is what we needed. The longer it’s 0-0, it gets harder and harder and harder.

[Where do you place your assist?]  It’s up there for sure. I spoke to Ant at half-time and said if I get into those half-spaces I’m looking to put it in so make sure you get to the back post. I didn’t expect it to work so quickly.

He’s a willing runner, great to play with him. I saw the run and was able to execute the pass,

It’s always a pleasure and an honour to represent my country. It’s been a long time. I’ve always believed that I can play for England and I want to. The manager’s given me the opportunity and I tried to do what he wanted me to do to the best of my ability and I hope he’s happy with how I played.

🦁 #1301Alex Scott reflects on a special night, earning his first senior England cap 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @gabrielclarke05 | @England pic.twitter.com/lC34bAPbbd

It was good, quite dominant. We created a lot of chances but without the quality. When they went a man down, we were too passive at times. We need to be dominant, as I said earlier, go for the throat and put teams away.

It’s my only header. I’d be the worst header of the ball you’ll ever see. Really happy, resally proud to score that because I can’t tell you the number of hours I’ve spent practising headers.

Perfectly competent and signs of promise in the left-back/left-wing axis. England looked too open against 11 men and better teams – hola España – may have capitalised on the sloppiness. But once Sulc was sent off, England gradually turned the screw and created a hatful of chances, running out easy winners.

Another tidy save from Kovar when Bellingham receives a pass from the left, strides towards the D, then drives a daisy-cutter towards the left of goal. The keeper swoops down early to turn it behind with a stiff wrist.

Two minutes of stoppage time are signalled as England try to pen the home side in their own half.

Ngumoha is enjoying himself and showing off some excellent close control.

Yes, for sure [this is as good as I’ve felt in an England shirt. My football IQ, I’m getting better and better, smarter and smarter. I need time to really feel at home, to feel comfortable and once I have that I don’t look back.

I knew exactly where I wanted to go, where I needed to go but I needed some guidance. I think the same way as him [Jude]. We don’t think there’s any limit on what we can achieve, wanting to win, wanting to win in a good way by going for the throat. Fearlessness.

It ate me up for a good couple of weeks after [losing the semi-final]. I’d scored… on the same pitch as Messi, the man I idolised as a kid. It was the highest possible moment of my entire life. And within 20 minutes it had come completely crashing down. There’s been a lot of controversy, a lot of talk about that. Going forward, if we are going to lose a game, it’s going to be like how we lost to Spain. We went for their throats, we missed a penalty and lost the game. But the way we went for them, no regrets. I want to stay as far away from that [regret] as possible.

[Did you ever think you would sign for Barcelona?] Yes. No one ever achieves anything in life by playing it safe. My personality is based on being bold, taking risks and going for whatever you want.

At this level we’re all as talented as each other but only the most mentally competitive and driven people can maintain success for a long time.

I always thought in England that people respected me because I was fast and I pressed but they never respected my quality and people are starting to take notice that I’m not just quick. In Barcelona if you’re not technical, if you’re not smart, you’d stand out like a sore thumb.

[Where do you see this squad in two years?] European champions.

The intensity we played with and the way we took it to the best team in the world [is what we’ve taken out of the Spain game]. We can be really proud of that. It was really good. Obviously tight margins decide games but overall we’re happy with the way we dusted the World Cup off and all that emotion.

Massively [relishing a run in the No 10 position in place of Bellingham]. I want to try and show what I can do in that role and make a positive impact.

The atmosphere here [is always intense] and they have a new coach. We’ve done our research. We have to respect them. It’s going to be difficult and it’s up to us to hold our nerve.

The Professional Footballers’ Association has leapt to Cole Palmer’s defence following his withdrawal from the England squad.

“When England see five players who need to withdraw when the single most proud moment a player has is to be called up for the national team, you just ask yourself, what’s wrong about the industry?” Molango said at the Fifpro performance summit in London.

“You see people like Cole Palmer, someone who would have played four consecutive summers in a row had he gone to the World Cup, and you wonder why is he missing?”He’s missing because he’s a victim of the calendar and that’s something that needs to absolutely trigger the alarm bells.”

Man City used ‘sham’ sponsorships in £830m cheating scheme

Manchester City arranged “sham” sponsorships in a near-£1bn plot to flout Premier League rules, an independent commission has found.

It was confirmed on Tuesday that City had been found guilty of all charges related to “serious breaches” of the league’s financial rules, with the commission also upholding all but one in relation to their failure to co-operate with an investigation spanning over three years.

The commission found that, of £949.94m City claimed in commercial income over a nine-year period, only £119.25m was legitimate, with the remaining £830.69m illicitly paid by their Abu Dhabi owners.

#1453. Carlo Rovelli says fundamental physics is overrated

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Chris Stokel-Walker is a freelance journalist in Newcastle, UK.

Carlo Rovelli is a physicist and writer whose research focuses on quantum theories of gravity. Credit: David Stock/eyevine

On the Equality of All Things: Physics and Philosophy Carlo Rovelli Allen Lane (2026)

Physicist Carlo Rovelli has spent much of his career working on the theory of quantum gravity, which seeks to reconcile quantum mechanics with the general theory of relativity. But, as he explores in his latest book, On the Equality of All Things, he is increasingly pondering an even bigger question: whether there is an ultimate description of reality at all.

I think physics is a fabulous enterprise, but the world is more complicated than just a fundamental equation. It is genuinely complex, which means that understanding the basic rules doesn’t tell us much about understanding the phenomena that we are interested in.

In the book, I say that fundamental physics is overrated. High-energy physics, particle physics, quantum gravity — it’s great science. I love it. It’s fantastic. It tells us something about the world. But stop thinking that it is the root of everything else.

Why bad philosophy is stopping progress in physics

Why bad philosophy is stopping progress in physics

My work is on quantum gravity, trying to write a theory that describes gravitational phenomena for which quantum theory cannot be disregarded. I find it super interesting because it pushes us to rethink reality. But I think it is a mistake to see physics as getting to the ultimate reality. The question of whether there is an ultimate reality is a bad question. ‘Ultimate’ doesn’t mean anything. Generality doesn’t mean better understanding.

I go running in the morning, and I try to run faster and faster. I have an objective to run faster, but that does not mean I want to reach the speed of light. In the same way, I want to know more about the world, but the very idea of knowing the ultimate reality seems an illusion and part of a world view that I think we should drop.

Yes, I think it does. I don’t think it is a particularly serious sin, but it has created problems for physics. Physicists have oversold the field, sometimes with good motivation. I think about theoretical physicist Stephen Hawking saying “philosophy is dead now”. This has created a colossal push against science, which I think is bad. People say: “Come on, you scientists pretended to be the arbiters of reality. You’re not.”

Physicists disagree wildly on what quantum mechanics says about reality, Nature survey shows

Physicists disagree wildly on what quantum mechanics says about reality, Nature survey shows

I think a lot of the physics literature is wasted, as well as some experimental efforts. Look how much experimental effort has been put into checking theories that then didn’t work. The most striking example has been supersymmetry (which predicts a partner particle for each of the basic building blocks of matter). How could the entire community be almost certain that a class of phenomena existed, only to have it shown empirically that it does not exist? We have to find the cracks in our knowledge, rather than making random choices.

Perspectivalism does not mean subjectivity. That is the point. There is nothing special about humans. We are just physical systems, like anything else. Yes, any account of reality needs to have a perspective, but it doesn’t need to be a human one. The Moon has one velocity with respect to Earth and a different velocity with respect to the Sun. It’s all relational. Not because there is a human observing it, but because velocity really is relative.

According to perspectivalism, people cannot formulate an ultimate description of reality.Credit: Getty

For me, the key is quantum mechanics. The theory works really well, but it is still confusing. There are several ways to make sense of quantum mechanics, and they can be divided into two classes. One involves theories that assume a framework of knowledge beyond what we can see (such as the many-worlds, universal-wave-function and hidden-variables theories).

The alternative, which I think is more scientifically fruitful and reasonable, says that quantum mechanics is telling us something deep about the world, namely that you should not ask what is really, really going on, because that’s a bad question.

One way would be to make an experiment that contradicts quantum mechanics. But it is often not crucial experiments that decide what we think is true. It’s a piling up of evidence. Some ways of thinking show themselves to be much more fruitful than others. Science is not only writing equations, checking predictions and discarding equations that give incorrect predictions. It also means evolving our general conceptual structure.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03626-7

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#1452. Celtic fans disgracefully boo during minute's silence on Remembrance Sunday: Referee ends tribute after just 13 SECONDS - even after warning from the PA announcer

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 03:28 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 04:51 EST, 9 November 2026

Celtic were forced to curtail plans to commemorate Remembrance Day after a section of their supporters booed during the planned minute's silence on Remembrance Sunday.

The Bhoys hosted Kilmarnock in the Scottish Premiership on Sunday - with Liam Scales' goal proving the difference in a 1-0 win.

However, ahead of kick-off at Parkhead, the annual tribute to the armed forces and their families was overshadowed by some fans' loud jeers.

As the players from both teams gathered around the centre-circle, an announcement on the public address system said: 'We will have a minute's silence today on Remembrance Sunday to remember all victims of all conflicts. We remember, in particular, the men who served Celtic football club and lost their lives at wartime.'

The audible disdain resulted in referee John Beaton being forced to cut the silence after just 13 seconds.

The noise was so palpable that the Celtic TV broadcast turned down the volume to try and minimise its impact too.

The minute's silence ahead of Celtic versus Kilmarnock was cut short due to some fans booing

Celtic TV turned down the volume to try and minimise the jeers during the curtailed silence

Referee John Beaton (right) cut the minute's silence after 13 seconds as a result of the booing

Furthermore, the lower tier of the standing section was empty until the Green Brigade and other fans started to file in from the concourse when referee Beaton’s whistle signalled the end of the tribute.

Football clubs across the United Kingdom observe a minute's silence with their nearest home fixture around Remembrance Sunday and Armistice Day - with the latter on November 11.

Many teams also wear poppies, something Kilmarnock wore on their strip, but Celtic didn't.

Some Celtic supporters refuse to partake in the tradition or actively take a stance against it, often citing the club’s Irish roots and linking it to the British Army‘s role in The Troubles.

Last season, in a quirk, Celtic hosted Kilmarnock on Remembrance Sunday too - with that minute's silence also cut short due to jeering. That time referee Don Robertson cut it short at 15 seconds.

As well as the booing in that match last term, some fans turned their back on the minute's silence and also made gestures.

Sunday's 1-0 win over Kilmarnock sees Celtic regain their four-point lead at the top of the Scottish Premiership.

It was under-pressure Martin O'Neill's side's first league win in their last three games.

Scales scored the only goal of the game on 26 minutes when he hooked a Camilo Duran cross into the top corner.

Celtic fans show their displeasure during the minute's silence for Remembrance Day in 2025

Celtic - and Kasper Hogh in particular - otherwise had a frustrating day in front of goal, with Benjamin Nygren missing a second-half penalty.

Hogh had an early goal disallowed as his barren run without a goal hit the 16-game mark since he netted a hat-trick at Kilmarnock on his second appearance.

Celtic have 31 points from their opening 13 matches - four more than bitter rivals Rangers who sit second but have a game in hand.

Kilmarnock remain rooted to the bottom of the table with nine points from 13 games - two adrift of 11th-place Aberdeen who have played a match fewer.

#1451. Russell must do something wacky now after disappointing Bahrain GP qualifying

Never mind the lack of an ice vest, George Russell is somehow going to need to be the coolest man in Malaysia if he is to turn seventh on the grid into a positive result in Sunday’s Bahrain Grand Prix.The first race in Sepang in nearly a decade – a late addition to the calendar because of the conflict in the Middle East – promises to be an absolute scorcher. It might even be worth setting your alarm for the 8am UK start time. Red Bull’s Max Verstappen will start in pole position for the first time this year. He will have Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton alongside him.

It will be the first time since Hungary 2023 that those two gladiators have started on a front row together. Throw in sweltering temperatures, low grip, high tyre degradation, and the ever-present threat of a Malaysian monsoon sweeping through Sepang, and you have the potential for fireworks.

Russell might need something wacky if he is to do anything from that far back. This was a desperately disappointing result for the British driver. After his victory in Baku last weekend, Russell was hopeful he had finally found the winning formula and that he could continue to take the fight to his team-mate Kimi Antonelli, whom he trails in the drivers’ championship by 66pts.

Eighth, four places behind, and 0.24sec slower than the Italian, was not what Russell would have had in mind, although both Mercedes drivers will rise a spot because of the five-place grid penalty meted out to Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar for exceeding his engine allowance for the season.Russell will have felt particularly disappointed as Antonelli only got one run in Q3 after using up a set of soft tyres when he made a mistake and went off track in Q2. He now trails his team mate nine-seven in qualifying head-to-head this year.“No to be honest,” Russell admitted when asked whether he knew why he was so slow. “This circuit is an outlier in terms of the abrasiveness of the tarmac.“The lap times seven years ago were six or seven seconds faster and at certain points on the track it feels like you are driving on gravel, which is the same for everyone, but it is clearly affecting us more than others.”Mercedes’ lack of performance was doubly unexpected because not only did they arrive here with a massive upgrade package, but Russell revealed this week that he and Antonelli were foregoing the cooling vests you see some drivers sporting on the grid, in favour of car performance.

Toto Wolff, the Mercedes team principal, admitted it was a head-scratcher. “Very difficult to understand,” the Austrian said. “We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we did not see all year, but then you can say it is very hot and the tarmac is different to all the [other] tracks. It looked really good this morning. We seemed to have, at least with Kimi, made a step in understanding. And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”

Still, both titles are in the bag so Wolff cannot be too unhappy. Russell is the one who will be really miffed. He really needs to be beating his team-mate pretty much every race weekend if he is to get his title hopes back on track.

At the front, the mood was somewhat different. Verstappen became the first non-Mercedes-powered pilot to take a pole position this year. It was a first pole position for Red Bull Powertrains, too. And with his long run pace looking more than decent, Verstappen should really hold on for his first win of 2026. Hamilton will do his best to hang on to the Dutchman’s coattails. The seven-time champion was delighted when told he had taken P2. “Let’s go guys! Finally! Great job guys, really great job. Car felt great.”

This was indeed an excellent performance from the Ferrari man – and just the tonic for the Scuderia after weeks of gossip and speculation. Hamilton was admittedly three tenths slower than his rival, which he put purely down to a power deficit on the straights, but he said he was hopeful his long run pace was more competitive. The last time a F1 held a race was held here back in 2017, the British driver claimed pole only to be overhauled by a youthful Verstappen. He will be desperate to turn the tables this time.

“It was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one change before qualifying and we hit the sweet spot,” he reflected afterwards. “I am so, so grateful. I will try my best to hold on to Max tomorrow, and if we are in the fight that would be awesome. I’ve been talking too much, but I guess you talk more when you are happy. It was my best lap of the year. It feels like I won, and I will give it everything tomorrow.”

It is Russell, though, who needs a result even more badly if he is to remain a factor in the championship. “As a team, we have yet to have a bad race this whole season and this was clearly a very bad qualifying for us,” he admitted, adding that “all the numbers” from the upgrade package suggested it was an improvement on the old car. “But I think there is going to be a lot happening tomorrow. The tyre deg is huge and race pace will be king. So even though today was a real disappointment it is not the be all and end all.”

No. 1 ☝️#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/01PqrckQS9

Tomorrow’s race will be the first time since Hungary 2023 that Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton will start on the front row together. It is a reasonable run down to turn one and there are overtaking opportunities through the first few corners at Sepang, with it being similar to the configuration in China, with plenty of lines and moves on offer.

Respect between two great champions 🤩#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/fbZ6aoKRyw

We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we did not see all year, but then you can say it is very hot and the tarmac is the different to all the (other) tracks. And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”

“The car has been very good since last week. It is good to come back [from his wrist injury] at such a time and I am enjoying it, fighting for the top three. Even though it was not my finest qualifying session it is a good feeling.

“It is a bit unfortunate we take a penalty on a track where we are that fast but, from eighth, I am confident we can come through the field and come back for a good result.”

What about Verstappen? The man who won here the last time we were in Malaysia continues his great form today and goes quickest by more than three tenths.

Antonelli now heads out and will have the track to himself really. This is going to be the championship leader’s only flying lap of Q3.

Russell is the first man to head out for his first flying lap in Q3. Antonelli has remained in the pits with just one new set of softs remaining. Verstappen, who right now feels like the favourite for pole, will be one of the last across the line in these first attempts of Q3.

The fight for pole position in Sepang begins now as the green light is on at the end of the pit lane to get Q3 going.

Antonelli, due to that lap time deletion in Q2, has just one new set of softs for Q3, which could prove costly in his attempts to try and take pole.

P12 the best qualifying result of the season for Alonso. It was only his second time in Q2 after Hungary (P16).

I should add, P14 was also Lance Stroll’s best qualifying result of the season. His first outing in Q2 this year.

11. Liam Lawson (Racing Bulls)12. Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin)13. Carlos Sainz (Williams)14. Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)15. Franco Colapinto (Alpine)16. Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls)

With grid penalties already on their way, neither Colapinto nor Lindblad set lap times in Q2.

Verstappen, Leclerc, Piastri, Norris, Hadjar and Russell all remain in the pits. A bit of a risk for Russell down in eighth but his time should be enough to get into Q3.

Lindblad, who will start tomorrow’s race at the back of the grid after penalties, gives his teammate Lawson a tow down the back straight and it works as Lawson just sneaks into the top ten.

Can Bortoleto get back ahead though of Lawson? Yes he can and he will take the final place in Q3. Lawson thought he might be through but the tow was not enough.

Lindblad, who's taking a grid penalty for Sunday's race, gave team mate Lawson a tow but it wasn't quite enough to send the Kiwi into Q3#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/IMlrqg4ENv

As the young Italian starts his flying lap, there is no-one else out on track so no traffic. He is a lot more cautious at turn six this time than last time, when he had his lap time deleted.

He has not set blistering first and second sector times but a purple final sector puts him into second and the Italian is safely into Q3.

Plenty of other drivers are now heading around the track for their final flying laps of Q2.

11. Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)12. Carlos Sainz (Williams)13. Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes)14. Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls)15. Franco Colapinto (Alpine)16. Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin)

Mercedes have put a brand new set of softs onto Antonelli’s car as he heads out promptly, with no lap time to his name so far. Antonelli is still disputing the lap deletion over team radio but his team tell him the images show he exceeded track limits. This is now a lot of pressure on the championship leader; any mistake now and he will not make Q3. His teammate Russell is only in seventh.

Antonelli was fourth fastest but has had his lap time deleted for exceeding track limits at turn six. That is a big moment in Q2 and could prove problematic if he gets into Q3. Antonelli appeared to be confused when he was told about his lap deletion over team radio but the on-board view looked pretty clear-cut.

Piastri then comes across the line in third.

Here's the moment Kimi ran wide 👀#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/E0VdWdBt8x

The Dutchman looks in a great spot at the moment to take pole position today and his 1:35.696 is very quick. He is nearly four tenths quicker than Antonelli.

How about the Ferraris? Leclerc was quickest in the middle sector but is nearly three tenths down on Verstappen. Hamilton puts himself into third place. Russell is more than half a second down on Verstappen.

Verstappen has been shown a black and white flag for driving unnecessarily slowly. I doubt he will get a grid penalty for that but it will be a warning for the Dutchman.

Anyway, the drivers, other than Colapinto and Alonso, are on flying laps, with Verstappen currently fastest inthe first sector.

The green light is showing at the end of the pit lane and the second part of qualifying is under way. Like the start of Q1, it is hardly a stampede to go out.

17. Nico Hulkenberg (Audi)18. Oliver Bearman (Haas)19. Esteban Ocon (Haas)20. Alex Albon (Williams)21. Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac)22. Sergio Perez (Cadillac)

The Aston Martin of Stroll improves significantly from 20th and is set to make Q2, as is his teammate Alonso. A bit of a surprise to see the Aston Martins improve and make it into Q2.

Go Fernando! 🤩 Go Lance! 🤩First double Q2 appearance this season 🙌#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/xjiWYv6ycr

That has seen the Audi of Hulkenberg drop into the drop zone and the German is out. For contrast, his teammate improves to go into eighth place! Hulkenberg had a big lock up into turn 14, which proved very costly.

As it stands, eight of the top nine are remaining in the garage. Russell is in ninth and has not gone out but Gasly above him in eighth has. You would imagine Russell is perfectly safe.

17. Esteban Ocon (Haas)18. Alex Albon (Williams)19. Oliver Bearman (Haas)20. Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)21. Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac)22. Sergio Perez (Cadillac)

Ocon, in 17th, is quite far off Hulkenberg in 16th and needs more than four tenths to usurp him.

The screens in the media centre here in Sepang tell me that the air temp right now is 32.8C and the track temp is 58C. It feels even hotter. Lots of chat about cooling vests this week, which are optional. George Russell is among the drivers who isn’t using one, which is interesting a) because Russell has suffered badly from heat in the past (Qatar, Singapore) and b) because he says Mercedes chose to put the development money into car upgrades instead.

It’s an interesting admission. Not everyone is sold on the idea of cooling vests. Ferrari and McLaren will definitely be using them this weekend, for instance. Max Verstappen won’t as he doesn’t like them. Russell thinks the FIA should just develop the tech themselves and it shouldn’t be part of the budget cap.

“Our team have put a lot of emphasis this year on the cockpit temperature,” he said. “We won’t be running the cooling vest because we haven’t put the resource into making it robust enough. I feel we need the FIA just to step in and say ‘Here’s some money extra in the cost cap or there’s an external company who’s going to develop it for everybody’. Because we should all be wearing it. When it works, it works great. So, I would like to wear it this week, and I would like to wear it next week. But the team asked me...look, we can develop it, and we can put the money towards it...[but at a cost].

He added: “The top itself is not expensive ..you’ve got to effectively make a system where you can fit a block of dry ice or actual ice, and then has the airflow to circulate the cool water throughout. If that system isn’t robust enough, then suddenly you have no circulation, and then you get hot. You get ambient temperature circulating. The vest is one-design, but the system that circulates the water is different [at different teams].”

The two Ferraris are on medium tyres but Leclerc still puts himself into second place. He is then displaced by Hamilton, who slots in behind Verstappen. Good times from the Ferraris on the mediums.

What about the McLarens? Norris goes sixth fastest but is more than six tenths down on Verstappen. Then comes Piastri, who goes fourth fastest, just under four tenths off Verstappen.

Arguably the three favourites for pole; Antonelli, Russell and Verstappen, are all on flying laps.

The first sector goes the way of Verstappen, who is purple, and then the Dutchman goes purple in the middle sector.

Antonelli is two tenths faster than his teammate Russell but Verstappen is over half a second quicker than the Mercedes. Hadjar is then second fastest to show the pace in the Red Bull this weekend.

Most of the teams waited and waited to come out and then suddenly lots of drivers are sent out, resulting in a queue in the pits! With the high track temperatures and high degradation, the drivers are crawling around on their out laps to preserve these soft tyres.

Bumper to bumper in the pit lane! #F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/ff8JO9kB1g

The two Haas drivers have a free track to themselves whilst everyone else bides their time. In theory, as the hour of qualifying goes on, the track temperature should decrease and the more rubber that is laid down the faster the track should get.

Finally, just before the two Haas drivers finish their first flying laps, the rest of the grid is starting to emerge, led by the Mercedes duo.

The green light is showing at the end of the pit lane and Q1 is officially under way. The two Haas drivers are the first to head out. Other than that, it is a quiet start to Q1.

The top four teams; Mercedes, Red Bull, Ferrari and McLaren, all have a genuine chance of taking pole in Sepang today. I think the true favourites though have to be the Mercedes duo and Max Verstappen but with how close it between all four of the teams you cannot rule anything out.

It is 33 degrees celsius air temperature, with the track temperature up at 58 degrees.

Not long to wait now until qualifying begins. It is hot, humid and dry in Sepang right now. As we know in Malaysia, the weather can change quickly and thunderstorms can roll in quite quickly but it looks like today’s qualifying will be a dry one. This will be one of if not the hottest qualifying sessions of the season, so much so that we are seeing umbrellas going up to get some shade from the sun rather than sheltering from any rain.

This will be important to consider after qualifying finishes as there will be some shuffling around:

Isack Hadjar (Red Bull): five-place grid penalty- new internal combustion engineFranco Colapinto (Alpine): ten-place grid penalty- new engineFranco Colapinto (Alpine): five-place grid penalty- causing a collision in BakuArvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls): back of the grid- complete power unit change

Hadjar has looked good since returning from his wrist injury so could be fighting it out near the front of the grid, although his five-place penalty will drop him down. We know Lindblad will be at the back and is very likely to be joined there by Colapinto, who is not going to be qualifying high up in the top ten in his Alpine.

Haas have announced that Frenchman Esteban Ocon will leave at the end of this season. Ocon now faces an uncertain future, with it difficult to see a spot for him on the F1 grid next season. There are suggestions that the 30-year-old’s replacement will be Brazilian Ferrari junior Rafael Camara, although nothing has been confirmed on that front. 21-year-old Camara currently leads the Formula 2 championship.

TGR Haas F1 Team and Esteban Ocon will part ways at the conclusion of the 2026 season. With plenty of racing ahead, our focus remains on working together to maximize every opportunity through to the final race of the year.#HaasF1 #F1 pic.twitter.com/4iQAuqnSyA

Aston Martin have now confirmed their driver line-up for next season, retaining both Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll. There had been reports that Alonso had been contemplating retirement but the 45-year-old will continue into another season.

Aston Martin Aramco confirms Lance and Fernando will continue as the team's drivers in 2027. Read more: ​https://t.co/ePyjJdyAIB pic.twitter.com/VogFUEbNxy

Other than the second seat alongside Ollie Bearman at Haas, the only other team to keep an eye on is Racing Bulls, with no definite confirmation on their exact driver line-up for next season.

Ferrari this week have publicly backed their team principal Frederic Vasseur, amid speculation over the Frenchman’s position and comments made by former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner, who said the job at Ferrari would be a “dream job”. Ferrari, who sit second in the constructors’ standings, have not won the drivers’ championship since 2007 (Kimi Raikkonen) and the constructors’ since 2008. Here is a snippet from Tom Cary’s piece on the matter:

In a hastily convened media call on Tuesday morning, Maria Conti, Ferrari’s chief communication officer, said the Scuderia had decided to issue a vote of confidence in Vasseur in response “not just to the story of Mr Horner, but in general, the speculation about Fred”.

“Ferrari has made its choices,” Conti said. “We have confidence – full confidence – in Fred Vasseur and in his team, and we continue to do so.

“At this time, it’s really important that the team remains united and cohesive, and we are focused with all the energy on the work ahead.”

“It is great to be back [in Malaysia]. I am really enjoying the track. We have had some wonderful races here over time. It is actually the 20th time we have been here, it started in 1999, and it is really exciting to be back. I really enjoyed getting out on the track and watching the cars closely.

“The drivers are super fit and they have some cooling but it is not easy. But you almost cannot get enough fluid through your body before your stomach gives up. Having this race and Singapore back-to-back increases that challenge.”

Especially with the big upgrade they have brought this weekend, Mercedes’ lead at the summit is looking unassailable right now.

Almost nine years ago to the day, Max Verstappen took just his second race victory in Formula 1. Lewis Hamilton, who took pole position, and Daniel Ricciardo joined Verstappen on the podium. Despite being nine years ago, plenty of drivers still on the grid were racing that weekend. Here they are and who they were racing for:

Max Verstappen (Red Bull) Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes) Valtteri Bottas (Mercedes) Esteban Ocon (Force India)Nico Hulkenberg (Renault)Sergio Perez (Force India)Fernando Alonso (McLaren)Lance Stroll (Williams)Carlos Sainz (Toro Rosso)Pierre Gasly (Toro Rosso)

With Russell winning in Baku and Antonelli finishing fifth, the latter’s championship lead was cut to 66 points. If Russell is going to usurp his teammate, he is going to need a few more similar results to last weekend due to the size of Antonelli’s lead. If Antonelli were to suffer a retirement, then that completely changes the outlook.

Formula One returns to Malaysia for round 16 of the season for the Bahrain Grand Prix. That probably sounds strange but after the Bahrain Grand Prix was originally postponed in March, F1 reinstated it to the calendar with Malaysia hosting it because of the ongoing war in the Middle East. Despite being held in Malaysia, Bahrain have retained the naming rights for the event, which is officially known as the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. The last time Formula One was in Malaysia was nine years ago back in 2017, when a young whippersnapper named Max Verstappen, still four years away from winning his first world championship, claimed just his second victory.

Last time out around the streets of Baku, Mercedes’ George Russell claimed victory at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, pipping Verstappen by just a tenth of a second. That was Russell’s first grand prix win since June and cuts his team-mate Kimi Antonelli’s lead in the drivers’ standings to 66 points. Antonelli had a challenging weekend in Baku, starting 16th after a crash in qualifying and coming home in fifth to see his championship lead to Russell cut by 15 points.

Verstappen was quickest in first practice yesterday, with the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc fastest in second practice. Earlier today, championship leader Antonelli was nearly three tenths clear of the field in third practice. Mercedes, 160 points clear at the top of the constructors’ standings, have brought significant upgrades this weekend, which includes a new floor, rear suspension and rear corner. It is the team’s first significant car update since the Canadian Grand at the end of May.

This race in Malaysia represents the second leg of the season’s first flyaway triple header, with the Singapore Grand Prix to come next weekend, so the demands on the teams and the drivers are incredibly high. Qualifying from Sepang gets under way at 9am (GMT).

#1450. Some are calling this 'Tuchel 2.0' and his latest squad does feel like that. Here's why England think a tilt at the European Championship is within reach, writes IAN LADYMAN

Published: 17:35 EST, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 05:45 EST, 9 November 2026

One of Thomas Tuchel’s favourite analogies when it comes to the development of his England team is that of a train leaving a station with only the chosen few on it. As time moves on, the bodies lying on the tracks are growing greater in number.

Consider this statistic. Of the 26 players who travelled to the World Cup in America 13 are not in the squad chosen by England manager Tuchel for next week’s Nations League games against Croatia and Spain. And that does not include Cole Palmer and Phil Foden who, after missing out in the summer, were expected by many of us to have forced a way back in by now.

Tuchel’s latest selection has been affected by injuries, of course. But more significant is that the experienced German believes he is now starting to see an England team and squad develop in a way and in a direction that even he hadn’t envisaged once Argentina ended his World Cup hopes in that dismal Atlanta semi-final in July.

Different feelings, different style of play and, to a degree, different players.

Some are calling this ‘Tuchel 2.0’ and it does feel a little bit like that. The start of the second phase of Tuchel’s tenure, the start of the road towards a tilt at another trophy, the European Championships of 2028.

Having admitted to some worry ahead of the four-game international break FIFA saddled us all with last month, Tuchel sat down yesterday looking and sounding like a man once again certain of himself.

Tuchel sat down with the media looking and sounding like a man once again certain of himself

The inclusion of Jobe Bellingham — Jude’s younger brother (right) — was the headline act but there were other messages written within

Certain enough of a direct, quick, athletic style of play that helped England to two wins over Czech Republic and one – by seven goals – against Croatia in Rijeka. And certain that a dependence on players like Jordan Henderson, Dan Burn and John Stones for what we may politely call ‘squad culture management’ lies now in the past.

All of this may crash down in Madrid next Sunday. Spain have already beaten Tuchel’s England once – at Wembley in late September – and a repeat this month would ask familiar questions about England against the really good teams.

But for now, Tuchel is confident enough to claim that he has found his path.

‘We said at some point we need to take the next step, to build on what we have, to get better and to improve otherwise you’re just left behind,’ said Tuchel yesterday.

‘That’s how football works. You have been champion in one season but you need to improve, you need to bring in new players for competition, young players, new energy, fresh energy. It’s also the way, naturally, the national team goes.

‘We cannot be stuck in the same personnel and in the same style of play.

‘I agreed with you last month. I was the first to admit I was not 100 per cent happy with the pure level of football we played in the US. I saw a higher level in training [than on the field], I saw a higher level in glimpses.

‘We adjusted some things tactically, created some new positions and took the next steps.’

The Tuchel we sat down with in late September still wore the scars of the summer’s disappointment – and the criticism that came with it – rather visibly. It was the first time we had seen him like that in his two years in the job. He was tetchy and easily provoked. Call it the Argentina effect if you like.

Here, he appeared rather healed. Good results tend to do that for a manager and a little time helps too. If he believes his team has moved on then maybe he has also and he had to.

Certainly, his selection squad speaks to that. The inclusion of Jobe Bellingham – Jude’s younger brother – was the headline act but there were other messages written within.

Henderson and Burn are available but not included. So too Arsenal’s Noni Madueke, excluded to the benefit of the more direct Liverpool winger Rio Ngumoha.

‘We need runners who will go between the lines,’ said Tuchel. A clear indication, there, that too much of England’s summer wing play was too slow and too conservatively narrow.

Palmer, Foden and Kobbie Mainoo are also on the outside looking in once again and the case of the Manchester United midfielder is perhaps indicative of how Tuchel now operates.

Moved to apologise to him in front of the whole squad in July for his lack of minutes at the World Cup, Tuchel was determined Mainoo would play in the opening four games of the Nations League campaign.

‘I was desperate to give him the minutes and desperate to include him in this new start,’ explained Tuchel.

‘But then he pulled out. He missed an excellent camp and also entered a difficult, difficult spell for himself.

‘Man United fell off a cliff a little bit performance-wise. So this is why he now suffers.’

We can talk about the whys and wherefores of that logic. If Mainoo was good enough in September then why is he not good enough now? How desperate could Tuchel really have been to play him that one withdrawal with injury closed the door for the next camp and opened it instead for Bellingham jnr?

This, though, is how Tuchel works. He is an adept tactician but he’s also a mood coach, someone who – after sobering club experiences at places like PSG, Chelsea and Bayern Munich – places huge emphasis on environments and gut feels and culture. If he feels something works, he doesn’t like to pick it apart without good reason.

This is why for example the growing voice and influence of Elliot Anderson has left Jordan Henderson suddenly surplus. Tuchel says the door is not closed on a player who will be 38 by the time the next Euros are played and he called him this week to say so. In Tuchel’s mind, though, England will now move without the veteran and others of his ilk.

‘I was concerned before the last camp that we missed the players who kept our standards,’ said Tuchel.

‘I was worried that we missed so many of them. But then this group found their own way and their own voices.

It’s also reasonable to ask why our head coach can’t find room in his squad – if not his team – for the game changing duo of Palmer and Foden

‘I know what the others did. They built a platform on which these ones can build.’

Time will tell. To a degree, Spain will tell. Can England play the kind of higher tempo, front foot football we saw against Croatia and the Czechs against the world and European champions next Sunday? They embarrassed us when we didn’t have the ball at Wembley.

It’s also reasonable to ask why our head coach can’t find room in his squad – if not his team – for the game-changing duo of Palmer and Foden. England lacked good substitutes at the World Cup. There was too much like for like.

England need to win in order for such decisions to be vindicated and Tuchel knows that.

Asked yesterday if he felt as invigorated as he looked he said he did. ‘The last camp gave me a lot of energy, gave me a lot of extra belief,’ he said.

‘It gave me a lot of optimism to not compromise on the way England teams should play. Be physical but also step up in the pure level of performances.’

It’s certainly time for this now. The summer only served to expose English shortcomings. Tuchel’s train must arrive in Madrid next weekend, not only with fresh personnel but also new ideas clearly apparent.

#1449. How to make failure your friend and teacher in science

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dom Byrne is a freelance radio and podcast producer based in Brighton, UK.

How can the apprenticeship model and its focus on practice making perfect apply to science?Your browser does not support the audio element.Download MP3See transcript

Roger Kneebone’s 2020 book Expert compares molecular scientists to Savile Row tailors, lacemakers to vascular surgeons. Kneebone, a former trauma surgeon who now leads a master’s programme in surgical education at Imperial College London, says the road to professional expertise begins with an “apprentice” phase, doing monotonous tasks repeatedly and learning from mistakes.

Ruth Morgan, a crime and forensic science researcher at University College London, says: “Whether you’re learning to do a titration in the lab, or whether you’re learning to cut material as a tailor, there are so many mistakes that you make in that process. And that’s kind of the point. Every time you make a mistake you get better, and there’s a huge amount of time spent doing that.”

Earlier this year, Morgan joined Kneebone at a conference session on failure and expertise, part of a one-day failure in science conference, held at Imperial College London in partnership with Nature.

In the fourth episode of a six-part podcast series that revisits some of the conference themes, Morgan says successful collaborations across scientific disciplines rely on individual researchers seeing themselves as “outsiders, beginners”, unafraid of asking questions. “That’s incredibly scary” she says, “because it means you have to concede that you don’t know something, and you’re having to ask.

“It’s quite a distinctive skillset to cultivate. You have to be willing to be uncomfortable, to really drill into what you know, but what you don’t know, and to become a really good listener, so that you can hear what somebody else in a different space sees or knows."

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03654-3

We talked about the taxonomy of failure and how that can look throughout the life cycle of expertise, as a necessary companion, and a teacher, that is on the journey with us as we go from being essentially an apprentice through to becoming more expert.

That’s Professor Ruth Morgan reporting back from the failure and expertise session in a conference held at Imperial College London, in April 2026.

We talked about intrinsic failure that seems to be inherent whenever you’re working at intersections, whether that’s an intersection of two different disciplines that maybe look at failure or perceive failure in different ways.

I’m Dr Stephen Webster, director of the Good Science Project at Imperial, a programme that examines what we like about research culture, and what we don’t.

In episode four of this series about failure in science, we explore the benefits and the pitfalls of being an expert in your field.

The thread that really brought all that together was this idea of the potential for failure and the pain.

So, the importance of the wrestle, which is a term I’ve been thinking about a lot recently.

We have to create spaces to be able to wrestle with an idea, with the potential for failure, with difference of perspectives, difference of opinion, different ways of seeing things.

The pain is there in both in the way they come together is quite deeply and profoundly part of being human, and part of innovation and discovery and curiosity.

So I’m Professor Ruth Morgan. I’m based at UCL and professor of crime and forensic science.

Anyone who’s been working in this kind of space for any length of time can think of far too many personal failures.

But I guess a very public one that I can share with you was when I set about trying to crowdfund a very large sum of money to build an evidence interpretation lab, which would have been the first one in the world.

And I actually even ended up working with a big advertising agency, and we had we had billboards on buses through London.

We had a film that was in every single independent cinema in the UK for four months, I think.

And it was incredible. It was a beautiful piece of storytelling, and we raised about £4.25. The target was a million, so we fell short there. So that was a fairly public failure.

So in the failure and expertise session that we had at the conference, our discussion was curated and led by Professor Roger Kneebone, who’s the author of the book Expert, and he talks very beautifully about this journey that you go on from being an apprentice, building your expertise to the point where you become an expert.

And one of the things that we really explored in that conversation was around how, when you’re learning as an apprentice, you have to do the same task again and again and again.

It’s very monotonous. And there’s a huge amount of failure involved in that.

So, whether you’re learning to do a titration in the lab, or whether you’re learning to cut material as a tailor, there are so many mistakes that you make in that process.

Every time you make a mistake you get better, and there’s a huge amount of time spent doing that.

And it’s only as you go through that do you start finding the little shortcuts and heuristics and ways of seeing it that you have gained through all of those failures, and to the point of then becoming able to then teach others and be seen as an expert.

So there’s this idea that failure becomes something of a companion as you go through that journey. And it’s absolutely intrinsic to building expertise, to gaining that craft.

So the Heurista Institute came about, we got to this idea that there are an awful lot of complex challenges in the world, and you could argue that in many ways they’re getting more complex.

So the more you can explore them, the more you know about them, actually, the more complex they get.

What if the answer to a lot of these problems is less about creating new knowledge, and it’s more about bringing together existing forms of knowledge, but in different ways, asking different questions, and making connections that maybe haven’t been made before that move us forward in a sort of stepwise change moment?

So it’s about how do we bring those different perspectives together, those different disciplines together, in a structure within a university which is quite delineated by disciplines, and those boundaries are often quite clear.

And also, how do we traverse and bridge the boundaries that exist with and around that university system, with industry, with government, with other sectors where that insight is needed, and who can actually do stuff with it and actually make a difference?

And so we, yeah, so that’s how the institute came about.

Can we bridge those gaps between disciplines, and can we bridge the boundaries that exist between the university and the real world?

One of the things that is extraordinary about working at these intersections between different disciplines is that it really opens up the opportunity to be an outsider, to be a beginner, and to ask questions.

And that’s incredibly scary, because it means you have to concede that you don’t know, you don’t know something, and you’re having to ask.

But it also levels the field, if you like, and it actually makes people more open to asking those questions and being challenged in ways that help you see things in different ways that you might not have been able to see in a different context.

So it’s quite a distinctive skillset to cultivate.

You have to be willing to be uncomfortable, to really drill into what you know, but what you don’t know, and to become a really good listener, so that you can hear what somebody else in a different space sees or knows.

And then start that translation work, of translating between those different perspectives.

One of the things that we’ve really noticed in the work that we do is that our sort of starting point was we want to bring all these different perspectives together so that we can find the points of resonance, the places where people agree, because that will really help us at these intersections, work out maybe where to go next.

So failure in that sense, I think, is very, very interesting because, in some ways, you’re having to unlearn everything you’ve learnt What it means to be an expert in a particular discipline, you have to be willing to put that down in some ways, and to come into a space that you don’t understand.

And what does it mean for trust in science? I think at the moment we’re really looking into a storm of events that really question expertise, trust in science.

And the challenge to the trust in the scientific process and new knowledge and evidence that it generates, I think, is a serious perspective around the erosion of social cohesion.

So, in the opening session, Professor Jen Woods was talking about this sort of post-trust world and this observation that there’s a lack of trust in experts and how, where that’s taking us as a society.

And I think it’s really, this is a really fascinating area, because there’s something here about the the contract that exists between science and society, and how that has changed.

So, if we think about 80 years ago, we had an understanding that governments would fund scientists.

They had a lot of freedom and autonomy, and there was a lot of trust there that what the scientists discovered would be valuable and would bring about good in society.

And we saw lots of things emerge from that. I think washing machines is a great example, for example.

But out of that also came some things that maybe were more questionable, people weren’t quite so sure about.

And there has been a notable shift in the way that society and science interact with each other, and you could argue that where we are today is much more of a transactional relationship, where there are certain needs in society that are put to the science community.

And those are the areas where we would like science to focus, to find solutions that will benefit society and often the country within which those scientists are working.

So I think that overarching change in the way that we work within society is quite interesting

And I think it speaks a lot about the value and importance of science being done with and for people, not to and at them.

And there’s also something very interesting then about this, is this role of experts, and this idea that there’s a production in trust in experts.

And I just find this very fascinating because what we mean by trust is quite variable.

So the work from the Pew Research Institute talks about, they do lots of surveys to look at where where is trust in society, and actually scientists are actually quite high up and they haven’t fallen hugely.

So other experts have lost trust, but scientists are still quite high up.

Where the trust goes down is when scientists are starting to get involved in policymaking.

So that’s the nuance here, that there’s trust in science and there’s trust in scientific experts.

But there’s less confidence when those experts are perceived to be moving outside of their specialist domain and into more applied settings.

So I think there’s something very important here about how do we navigate a world where we believe that science has a huge amount to offer society, where science embedded into the way that we build our societies is going to add value and bring about things that we would want to uphold in society.

But how do we do that in a way where there is dialogue and transparency in terms of what can science do, what questions can it ask, what answers can it give, and not overstretch or end up putting science in a place where it probably isn’t meant to be.
